keyVerseText: Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments, and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also his coat: now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout . woven: or, wrought
rootMeaning: The Greek adjective ἄῤῥαφος (árrhaphos) derives from the negative particle Α and a root related to ῥάπτω, meaning 'to sew.' Thus, its literal meaning is 'without seam,' indicating something not sewn together but made in one continuous piece. This etymology highlights the idea of unity and indivisibility, going beyond the simple English gloss to emphasize the seamless and unbroken nature of the object described.
usageInScripture: This word appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in John 19:23, where it describes a garment 'without seam.' The consistent translation as 'without seam' underscores the singularity and unstitched character of the garment, emphasizing that it was woven in one piece. This unique occurrence points to a very specific and deliberate use of the term to convey an object of particular craftsmanship and symbolic significance.
theologicalSignificance: The concept of 'without seam' carries profound theological weight, especially in relation to Christ. It speaks to the perfect unity and integrity of Jesus, who is whole and indivisible in His person and work. The seamless garment metaphorically reflects the unity of the church as the body of Christ, undivided and complete in Him. Understanding ἄῤῥαφος as 'unsewed' invites believers to appreciate the flawless and unbroken nature of Christ’s sacrifice and the perfect craftsmanship of God’s redemptive plan.
keyVerseReflection: John 19:23 describes how the soldiers divided Jesus' garments but noted that His coat was 'without seam, woven from the top throughout.' The use of ἄῤῥαφος here highlights the garment’s unique construction, symbolizing the unity and wholeness of Christ even in His suffering. This detail enriches the narrative by pointing to the intentional preservation of something whole and unbroken, paralleling the unbreakable nature of Christ’s person and mission.
